A great week on paper can hide a bad day on the eval. That's why my two logs never mix.

Every paper trade I take goes in one. Every evaluation trade goes in the other.

When they share a page, the totals blur together, and you walk away thinking the plan is working better than it is.

Paper is where I test an idea with nothing at risk. The eval has hard rules, a drawdown limit and the pressure that comes with it. Those are different conditions, so they get different scorecards.

At night I grade each one on its own and ask both the same question: did I follow the plan?

Save this if your journal lumps everything together.

instagram_1230:
Your stop is a plan. Your fill is what you get.

On 1 ES, a 4-point stop is $200 of planned risk. In a fast move, that exit can come in 2 points worse, and the same trade costs you $300.

So I size for the slip, not the perfect fill:
- leave room in your daily max for a worse exit
- pick a size where a bad fill still fits the plan
- if the slip doesn't fit on ES, drop to MES at $5 a point

Keep this one saved for Monday.

Some mornings the best move of the day is over before 10 AM, and I don't take it.

My rule is no trades before 10 AM Eastern. If ES makes its move before then, I miss it and wait for the next setup.

That costs me trades. It also keeps me out of the fastest minutes after the open, when chasing feels easiest.

I read the market better once that first rush settles. A missed move costs nothing. A chased one usually does.

Follow along for more of the rules I trade by.
